Somethings this article doesn't mention that contributes:

We're usually not well payed, but are sometimes required to be available 24/7.

We're often considered a money sink as opposed to an org that makes money so our budgets are minimal and often cut to fund other, money making, projects. This also means that our "projects" are expected to be low cost and stable which usually doesn't work.

Because end users are stupid, we're often told to lower security policies or introduce security vulnerabilities to ease the use of systems.

Our expertise is often ignored by CTOs and CEOs. Do you desperately need a way to back up your critical systems? Well you won't need one as long as you do your job and ensure they don't fail!

Tech departments really need a "secretary" of sorts that will help keep up with documentation as we're usually running around fixing problems and documentation gets pushed back or never done.

Everything is our fault always. Lightbulb died in the projector? Our fault. Printer ran out of toner? Our fault. Servers hit with a DDoS? Our fault. Cryptolocker unleashed because someone opened a zip file in their email? Our fault. Someone forgot a password? Our fault.

I can't think of any other department in any organization that is expected to take crap, have their budgets cut, be available 24/7, be under payed, be under staffed, know everything, fix everything, and do all of it with a smile on their face with the possible exception of nurses.
The fact that IT is usually a subgroup under accounting, doesn't help. I have found the typical accouting execs to be the most short sighted people in any organization.
Someone correct me if I'm wrong - but the solution they presented to this was to fire the unhappy people, and fire the few who did make it further up the ladder? That should improve morale!
